sample_q_texts: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) at scales beyond individual genomes have become an important resource for genetic studies, but their power is limited by the potential for biases in the original discovery signals. Besides batch effects, the accumulation of new variants with uninformative or limited effects can lead to spurious discordance in association signals. Given the increasing number of read genomes, detecting long-range association signals will be increasingly important for GWAS in de-novo gene discovery. To identify these potential long-range associations, methods combining association and genotyping data are generally used. However, these methods often suffer from limitations such as unwanted long-range associations, spurious long-range effects, and high false positives. In this work, we propose two novel genotype-informed methods for identifying long-range associations: data-driven LD (DL<sup>D</sup>) and ancestor-aware DL (ADDL). In DL<sup>D</sup>, the global LD-like association signals are mapped to individual genome-wide association signals within the set of haplotypes that were discovered. In ADDL, LD effects are considered for non-contiguous associations within individual GWAS datasets. Our analyses and experiments provide insights into the effectiveness of DL<sup>D</sup> and ADDL in identifying long-range associations. A more fine-grained understanding of the effects on genotypes for each individual by using our methods can help identify potentially informative DL signatures.

It is known that individual genes drive disease variation in the U.S. population. However, little is known about the underlying mechanisms. Researchers commonly assess diversity in population-specific genotypes at a single DNA variant, and it is often unclear what this variation within individuals is based on. We leveraged population-specific genotypes in one whole-genome dataset of 400,000 participants in the UK Biobank to quantify loci with real-world natural history. We performed population-specific single nucleotide variants comparisons to assess the transmission of genotype into individuals, test for causal common genetic variants, and identify genes responsible for rare occurrence within populations. We then explored the genetic composition of both rare and common variants in individuals.

An estimated 50 million genomes (7%) of the 400,000 participants in UK Biobank were genome-wide DNase-seq sequenced. From these, we measured 3,899,057 variants spanning 531 million primary ancestry individuals. More than 95% of common variants were clustered in individuals, and 95% of rare variants were in individuals. Most common alleles were homozygous. Rare alleles were more commonly not in individuals, or recessive, or were homozygous. If a genome-wide association study or associated signature were performed to identify each rare allele, 55% of all rare alleles would become common. At this locus, variants have many potentially functional outcomes, and are particularly likely to arise in somatic cells.

We additionally estimated the frequency of variant frequency and causal variants. More than 2% of alleles at this locus had the genotype at two different loci of affected relatives, suggesting a high likelihood of reciprocal gene(s) or causal variants. Potential deleterious causal variants in this locus were detected but a causal allele was not identified in two thirds of reported cases, implying somatic genetic variation in affected relatives. Most variants had a minor impact on average genotypes in general, supporting previously observed dominance and common transmission. We identified five genes with independent roles in producing rare and common variants, including genes in DNA repair, chromatin interaction, and synaptic plasticity.

Genotyping by sequencing (GBS) is a growing tool to identify rare alleles, correcting a high proportion of a family's recessive traits. However, for outliers with complex pedigrees, matching allelic profiles against reference population may be required to detect secondary selective sweeps. We compared the performance of the GBS pipeline and run a nucleotide polymorphism repeat probe library screening run on the GWAS meta-analysis data sets of the US and UK samplings with the candidate selection inference and blocking approach. The test set from the GBS pipeline had higher R2 fit values (0.79 compared to 0.30), but had less power to find more complex selection events. The R2 of the SNP-based duplicate warning option was higher for the UCL data set, but worse power for the different candidates test used. The R2-splithove estimate for the ghtr candidate, the candidate performing worst, increased with both the number of variants selected and the number of candidate selectors. The data included an additional poly-genic trait which acted as a modifier to the SNP test. The data from GWAS meta-analysis included another novel trait, the functional effect of which was entirely independent of the other traits. GBS can be useful for genotyping out-liers with various complex pedigrees, but caution is advised for cases where the precision of the performance is low.

The emergence of rapidly diverging genomes poses challenges to all of the disciplines in the field of human genetics. Efforts to overcome this challenge range from developing more accurate genetic variations to isolating patterns of genotype-phenotype correspondence. Whole-genome sequencing can provide a large number of informative bases for these studies and its largest datasets are publicly available, but inferring the evolutionary significance of these bases has long been an important and fruitful question. In this study, we devised and used in silico tools to accelerate and expand analyses of the Francis Crick database of whole-genome sequences of chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas, and other great apes. These analyses revealed enrichment for nucleotides that we can model with models of human genetic diversity and more efficient rules for detecting concordance between reference and variant genomes. Furthermore, we conducted validations to ensure the reliability of these alignments and models to uncover discordance in the models and various observed patterns of genotype-phenotype correspondence. In the final analyses, we used our models to identify the co-occurrent and non-co-occurrent orthologues of several novel genes of the deep-human genome project and to elucidate the roles of several predicted potential genes of the deep-human genome in mitochondrial metabolism. Our methods provide a highly efficient pipeline to accelerate and expand comparative analyses of deep human genomics.

The Genome-wide Association Study (GWAS) is a powerful tool to identify genetic variants that increase susceptibility to disease. However, to do so, the right variant must be extracted from tens or hundreds of millions of variants in the genome. The choice of optimal variant is often overlooked. We propose a straightforward yet principled approach, known as Variant Balanced Ranking (VBR), for predicting the suitability of variants as informative for drug response. We also discuss variants distribution from whole-exome sequence data to characterize the variance of variants across all targets. These variants form robust features in downstream analyses to identify drug-sensitive variants. VBR has been employed by several groups, but we discuss its technical challenges and inefficiencies, especially regarding the variants rank. One possible reason is that the current approach relates variant rank to the variant quality score, a heuristic measure suggested for estimating the benefit of a variant. The resulting variants rank may not be optimal for identifying drug-susceptible variants. Instead, we propose variants scoring based on multiple metrics and provide interpretable predictions. Furthermore, we discuss variants distribution across thousands of human genes in whole-exome datasets with accurate and precise information. We also discuss practical applications such as weight estimation in inverse propensity enrichment analysis (IPEA) and other multi-variant association studies (MVAS). Finally, we show that the VBR approach improves predictive power compared to approaches without variant rank.

Population genomic variation as a function of geographic location is one of the most pressing human genetic questions of our age. Recent technological advances have allowed us to measure any region of the genome to sub-kb resolution and estimate allele count with high accuracy. We propose to improve the prediction accuracy for regions containing intronic regions. Existing methods rely on positional summary statistics (PSSs) or pressure-based methods, but neither is capable of distinguishing background genomic drift on a scale of tens of kilobases. This study uses correlated observations across genetic distances from multiple genome-wide association studies to produce a new class of expansion modules (EMs) (n=100 million loci across 387 datasets) with strong positional association to candidate genome regions with relatively low genotype sequence complexity. EMs are components of a new classification of genomic features, aligning with and improving methods for genome-wide association studies of Mendelian and multifactorial traits. Our study reveals that the three major genomic modules have different associations with disease and trait. The EMs can be applied to GWAS including marker-trait associations, gene-trait association studies, and longitudinal studies. We validate its performance and demonstrate how EMs can be scaled to and incorporated into large-scale GWAS studies. Finally, we provide the draft resources used for applying the EM algorithm for GWA gene associations.

Recent developments in genomic sequencing technologies and genome wide association studies (GWAS) have shown the existence of pleiotropy, i.e. common, multiple genetic variant loci affecting multiple traits. This is particularly striking in human somatic, complex traits including metabolic, cancer, and mental health diseases, and genomic diversity has been interpreted as a major driver of these pleiotropy. In the brain, however, there are compelling cases of pleiotropy for neuropsychiatric traits, suggesting that genome-wide individual gene differences may not be enough to explain pleiotropy. Another popular explanation posits that heritable differences are caused by large-scale epigenetic modifications in the genome that are replicated many times, but are simply copied. However, this theory does not explain pleiotropy in the inherited common variants that affect the brain. Using bulk RNA sequencing and perturbation, we found novel clades of common polymorphisms for 11 major brain regions involved in cognition, motor, movement, and emotion, all affected by the same set of multiple variants. Transcriptomic approaches were used to measure the importance of these variants in mediating pleiotropic differences with the 11 significant classes of variants. Based on the number of affected variation across the regions, we identified three candidate regions that may control the expression of significant variants. These include the first-ever genome-wide data on significant genetics at the age of 3 years, using epigenetic information across 5500 SNPs. Our finding reveals the need to investigate molecular variants in both DNA and RNA.

Many complex traits are generated by the integration of many independently derived mutations. The identification of integrated mutations within individuals using such mutational evidence has been a long standing goal. Here, we present iGen: Integration Networks Analysis using Genomics (iGen), an integrated repository of mutations and evidences from all sequenced genomes. iGen consists of a powerful web-based tool that allows researchers to search multiple publicly available datasets for mutations that have been integrated into any single lineage or across multiple lineage-specific components. iGen allows users to search for elements of ancestry between two genomes, lineages, through time, or the entire superorganism. iGen also allows researchers to perform relational, causal, and behavioral analyses in an integrated manner. We provide comprehensive data on all genomic evidence in humans and demonstrate iGen's power in refining our understanding of human inheritance patterns by integrating knowledge on the natural variations within and across genomes. Importantly, iGen's secure, customizable, and open-source platform enables collaboration, deployment, and use across labs, data centers, and the world. To date, iGen has captured ~12,000 unique and unique evidence markers from 1,385 genomes. We encourage full integration of iGen into the growing pool of genomic data.

The conservation of sequence variants between taxa can be useful for the investigation of selection pressures, in addition to whole genome sequence data. We identified the "local heterogeneity" (LH) within a non-synonymous nonsynonymous SNP dataset of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and characterized the variation patterns in yeast based on the two-dimensional statistical maps of the LH. The LH plots highlighted recurrent genetic polymorphisms in yeast, with higher overlap values in nonsynonymous and synonymous sites in comparison to the synonymous and non-synonymous genes separately. Pairwise, haplotype-level covariation analysis of repeated SNPs showed overlapping groups of LH clusters for the same pair of genes as observed in yeast. The inclusion of LH as a trait-marker allows studies of variant-trait relationships and the classification of phenotype and genotype-phenotype relationships.

Highlights
Hierarchical dimension reveals variation patterns with higher overlap between local heterogeneity (LH) and local sequence diversity (LSD).

This study uses a yeast-specific dataset to identify genomic regions of varying complexity associated with putative complex human disease, represented by three monogenic, 20, or 135 kilobase segments (M, T22-TEF22-UDNH, and T37-UDNH) in non-synonymous sites for seven more complex human disease associated SNPs.

Classifying the genomes into groupings of sites segregated on pairwise divergence support an evident hidden layer of divergent sites.

Ordered arrays of coding sequences and prediction of the 5' cap might be useful to place the genetic heterogeneity within monogenic variation domains.

Systematic genetic disease screening approaches to predict pleiotropy from single base substitutions (mRNA-SNPs) have been successful at 70-80%, but correlate poorly with the clinical phenotype. To extend these successes and improve mapping to clinical phenotype, this study uses a set of brain-related genomic target genes that are likely associated with more frequent disease than previously reported. Using multi-species computational de novo gene finding pipeline, we generated a set of thousands of brain-specific large scale multi-sequence Genotyping and De Novo Gene Finding algorithms, using a neurodegenerative screen to predict specific human brain-specific and rare brain-specific targets. This data-augmentation greatly improves the robustness and accuracy of the resulting individual target gene screens. A clinical cohort of 799 people with a neurodegenerative disease was used to further verify the results and validate how well the predicted novel genes correlated with clinical phenotypes, demonstrating high accuracy for many genes including hits which then made their way to later more refined initial I/O calling. This process increased the estimated sensitivity by ~2.7-times, with a small increase in specificity. Further refinement and fine-tuning of the algorithm shows that most of the best genes for certain genes still remain, as seen in recent publications [1]. Therefore, in this study, we propose a new biologically motivated Genomic Disease Screening approach, which predicts the majority of human brain-specific gene targets by combining results from several previously documented pairs of brain-specific GDBs and Human mRNA-SNP hit pairs.

Understanding how genetic variants drive phenotypic differences is a major challenge in molecular biology. Single nucleotide polymorphisms form the vast majority of genetic variation and play critical roles in complex, polygenic phenotypes, yet their functional impact is poorly understood from traditional gene-level analyses. In-depth knowledge on the impact of single nucleotide polymorphisms has broad applications in health and disease, population genomic or evolution studies. The wealth of genomic data and available functional genetic tools make Drosophila melanogaster an ideal model species for studies at single nucleotide resolution. However, to leverage these resources and potentially combine it with the power of functional genetics to enhance genotype-phenotype research, it is essential to develop techniques to predict functional impact and causality of single nucleotide variants.

Here, we present FlyCADD, a functional impact prediction tool for single nucleotide variants in D. melanogaster. FlyCADD, based on the Combined Annotation-Dependent Depletion (CADD) framework, integrates over 650 genomic features - including conservation scores, GC content, and DNA secondary structure - into a single metric reflecting a variants predicted impact on evolutionary fitness. FlyCADD provides impact prediction scores for any single nucleotide variant on the D. melanogaster genome. We demonstrate FlyCADDs utility with some examples of application, including the ranking of phenotype-associated variants to prioritize variants for follow-up studies, evaluation of naturally occurring polymorphisms, and refining of CRISPR-Cas9 experimental design. FlyCADD provides a powerful framework for interpreting impact of any single nucleotide variant in D. melanogaster, thereby improving our understanding of genotype-phenotype connections.

Article summarySingle nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), the most common form of genomic variation, play key roles in micro-evolution and adaptation. In Drosophila melanogaster, many SNPs have been associated to phenotypes through association studies, yet functional validation remains challenging and experimental evidence for functional impact is rare. Here, we present FlyCADD, an impact prediction tool that integrates high-quality D. melanogaster genome annotations into a single score reflecting predicted impact of a SNP. FlyCADD can be applied to distinguish causal from neutral variants, for variant prioritization prior to functional studies, and to enhance interpretation of natural variation, thereby improving our understanding of genotype-phenotype relationships.

The nature of standing genetic variation remains a central debate in population genetics, with differing perspectives on whether common variants are mostly neutral or have functional effects. We address this question by directly mapping the fitness effects of over 9,000 natural variants in the Ras/PKA and TOR/Sch9 pathways--key regulators of cell proliferation in eukaryotes--across four conditions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. While many variants are neutral in our assay, on the order of 3,500 exhibited significant fitness effects. These non-neutral variants tend to be missense and affect conserved, more densely packed, and less solvent-exposed protein regions. They are also typically younger, occur at lower frequencies, and more often found in heterozygous states, suggesting they are subject to purifying selection. A substantial fraction of non-neutral variants showing strong fitness effects in our experiments, however, is present at high frequencies in the population. These variants show signs of local adaptation as they tend to be found specifically in domesticated strains adapted to human-made environments. Our findings support the view that while common variants are often neutral, a significant proportion have adaptive functional consequences and are driven into the population by local positive selection. This study highlights the potential to explore the functional effects of natural genetic variation on a genome scale with quantitative fitness measurements in the laboratory, bridging the gap between population genetics and functional genomics to understand evolutionary dynamics in the wild.

From a mathematical perspective, a genome can be viewed as categorical data whose elements include genetic variants in SNPs. Then, the problem of predicting phenotype from genotype can be reduced to the problem of classifying categorical data. We will define a metric function at each SNPs position of an individual such that the arithmetic mean of a specific phenotype group is always less than or equal to that of the comparison group. Then, in light of a mathematical principle, calculating the sum of the distances(metrics) of some SNPs positions could clearly classify the two groups, when difficult to classify them with one specific position.

Using this methodology, we found that even small differences in each SNPs combined could classify phenotypes ; combining 51 SNPs positions in autosomes made possible to distinguish males from females with great accuracy. We also found that East Asian people could be distinguished from other people with 100% accuracy, so we obtained a mathematical definition of East Asian people.

The mathematical methodology classifies phenotypes with collecting small differences of genotypes throughout the entire genome, which could be useful for predicting diseases affected by the genome and be useful in pharmacogenomics.

The importance of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) in numerous biological processes, including DNA synthesis and cellular energy production, underscores the need for therapeutic and public health strategies to address B12 insufficiency/deficiency in the population. Genetic variations in pathways influencing cobalamin absorption, transport, and metabolism can affect various direct and indirect measures of vitamin B12 status. To facilitate a structured approach to studying these genetic factors, we aimed to systematically curate and create a user-friendly web database that offers comprehensive data on genetic variants influencing B12 biomarkers. A Pubmed search was performed for 5 B12 traits (total serum/plasma B12, holotranscobalamin (active B12), total transcobalamin, holo haptocorrin, and methylmalonic acid) resulting in 493 research publications, of which 47 relevant publications were reviewed further. The database backend was built using MongoDB and the web interface was coded in PHP, JavaScript, HTML and CSS on an Apache HTTP server. We have manually curated and compiled the Cobalamin Associated Genetic Variant (CobVar) database, comprising a total of 324 genetic variant associations for 5 different vitamin B12 traits involving 222 unique genetic variants and 84 genes identified across several genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and candidate gene studies. About one-third of the total genetic variant associations have been reported in >1 independent studies and 15 variants in >1 ethnic group. FUT2 gene showed the maximum number of associations for total serum/plasma B12 (N=39), followed by MTHFR (N=24) and TCN2 (N=23). The database is accessible online at https://datatools.sjri.res.in/VBG/. CobVar is a vital resource for researchers and nutritionists, offering quick access to the latest developments in B12-related genetic variant research and serves as a valuable tool for advancing personalized treatment.

Database URLhttps://datatools.sjri.res.in/VBG/.

Microbial genome-wide association study (GWAS) tools often require manual data processing steps, lack comprehensive workflows, and are limited by scalability issues, thus hindering the exploration of bacterial genetic traits. To address these challenges, we developed BaGPipe, an automated and flexible bacterial GWAS pipeline built using Nextflow and incorporating Pyseer for association analysis. BaGPipe integrates all essential components of a bacterial GWAS--spanning pre-processing, statistical analysis, and downstream visualisation--into a unified workflow that is reproducible and easy to deploy across diverse computational environments. BaGPipe was validated on a publicly available dataset of Streptococcus pneumoniae whole-genome sequences, and reproduced published findings with improved computational efficiency. BaGPipe was then applied to a dataset of Staphylococcus aureus whole-genome sequences, successfully identifying known and novel antibiotic resistance associations. By offering an accessible, efficient, and reproducible platform, BaGPipe accelerates bacterial GWAS and facilitates deeper exploration into the genetic underpinnings of phenotypic traits.

Impact StatementThe increasing availability of bacterial genome sequences has created an opportunity for robust, reproducible tools to facilitate the discovery of novel genotype-phenotype associations. Despite the demonstrated utility of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in identifying genetic determinants of disease, toxicity and antibiotic resistance, existing tools for bacterial GWAS often involve fragmented workflows requiring extensive manual intervention, limiting their adoption and reproducibility. Here, we introduce BaGPipe, a fully integrated bacterial GWAS pipeline that automates pre-processing, statistical analysis, and visualisation, thereby streamlining the entire workflow. With its flexibility, scalability, and ease of use, BaGPipe makes bacterial GWAS more accessible to researchers, enabling faster and more reliable insights into microbial genetics. This is an important step towards overcoming the computational and logistical barriers that have constrained bacterial GWAS, ultimately accelerating research into microbial evolution, resistance mechanisms, and the genetic basis of other key phenotypic traits.

Data SummaryBaGPipe is freely available at https://github.com/sanger-pathogens/BaGPipe. The Streptococcus pneumoniae input dataset is available from the Pyseer tutorial (https://pyseer.readthedocs.io/en/master/tutorial.html#). The Staphylococcus aureus sequencing assemblies can be sourced from their ERS accession numbers provided in supplementary data. The reference assemblies, listed in the supplementary, can be sourced from NCBI.

Conventional genome mapping-based approaches systematically miss genetic variation, particularly in regions that substantially differ from the reference. To explore this hidden variation, we examined unmapped and poorly mapped reads from the genomes of 640 human individuals from South Asian (SAS) populations in the 1000 Genomes Project and the Simons Genome Diversity Project. We assembled tens of megabases of non-redundant sequence in tens of thousands of large contigs, much of which is present in both SAS and non-SAS populations. We demonstrated that much of this sequence is not discovered by traditional variant discovery approaches even when using complete genomes and pangenomes. Across 20,000 placed contigs, we found 8,215 intersections with 106 protein coding genes and >15,000 placements within 1 kbp of a known GWAS hit. We used long read data from a subset of samples to validate the majority of their assembled sequences, aligned RNA-seq data to identify hundreds of unplaced contigs with transcriptional potential, and queried existing nucleotide databases to evaluate the origins of the remaining unplaced sequences. Our results highlight the limitations of even the most complete reference genomes and provide a model for understanding the distribution of hidden variation in any human population.

One key component of study design in population genetics is the "geographic breadth" of a sample (i.e., how broad a region across which individuals are sampled). How the geographic breadth of a sample impacts observations of rare, deleterious variants is unclear, even though such variants are of particular interest for biomedical and evolutionary applications. Here, in order to gain insight into the effects of sample design on ascertained genetic variants, we formulate a stochastic model of dispersal, genetic drift, selection, mutation, and geographically concentrated sampling. We use this model to understand the effects of the geographic breadth of sampling effort on the discovery of negatively selected variants. We find that samples which are more geographically broad will discover a greater number variants as compared geographically narrow samples (an effect we label "discovery"); though the variants will be detected at lower average frequency than in narrow samples (e.g. as singletons, an effect we label "dilution"). Importantly, these effects are amplified for larger sample sizes and moderated by the magnitude of fitness effects. We validate these results using both population genetic simulations and empirical analyses in the UK Biobank. Our results are particularly important in two contexts: the association of large-effect rare variants with particular phenotypes and the inference of negative selection from allele frequency data. Overall, our findings emphasize the importance of considering geographic breadth when designing and carrying out genetic studies, especially at biobank scale.

SignificanceAs genetic studies grow, researchers are increasingly seeking to identify rare genetic variants with large impacts on traits. In this paper, we combine theoretical methods and data analysis to show how differences in sampling with respect to geographic location can influence the number and frequency of genetic variants that are found. Our results suggest that geographically broad samples will include more distinct genetic variants, though each variant will be found at a lower frequency, as compared to geographically narrow samples. Our results can help researchers to consider the implications of study design on expected results when constructing new genetic samples.

The Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) is a foundational resource for allele frequency data, widely used in genomic research and clinical interpretation. However, traditional estimates rely on individual-level genetic ancestry groupings that may obscure variation in recently admixed populations. To improve resolution, we applied local ancestry inference (LAI) to over 27 million variants in two admixed groups: Admixed American (n = 7,612) and African/African American (n = 20,250), deriving ancestry-specific allele frequencies. We show that 78.5% and 85.1% of variants in these groups, respectively, exhibit at least a twofold difference in ancestry-specific frequencies. Moreover, 81.49% of variants with LAI information would be assigned a higher gnomAD-wide maximum frequency after incorporating LAI, potentially altering clinical interpretations. This LAI-informed release reveals clinically relevant frequency differences that are masked in aggregate estimates and may support reclassifying some variants from Uncertain Significance to Benign or Likely Benign.

Interbreeding between anatomically modern humans and archaic hominins has contributed to the genomes of present-day human populations. However, our understanding of the specific gene regulatory consequences of Neanderthal, and particularly, Denisovan introgression is limited. Here, we used a massively parallel reporter assay to investigate the regulatory effects of 25,869 high-confidence introgressed SNPs segregating in present-day individuals of Papuan genetic ancestry in immune cell types. Overall, 8.22% of Denisovan and 8.58% of Neanderthal sequences showed active regulatory activity, and 9.22% of these displayed differential activity between alleles. We examined the properties of active and differentially active sequences, and found no impact of introgressed allele frequency on the probability of activity, but do observe an association with distance to the nearest transcription start site. Differential activity was also associated with differential transcription factor binding. Genes predicted to be regulated by differentially active sequences included IFIH1 and TNFAIP3, key immune genes and known examples of archaic introgression. Overall, this work provides insight into the regulatory activity of archaic variants in Papuan populations and, more broadly, the contribution of archaic introgression in shaping modern human genetic diversity.

Using genotype data consisting of 8,316 individuals, we systematically evaluated imputation performance across six state-of-the-art reference panels for Chinese and Thai populations. A substantial proportion of variants identified through whole-genome sequencing, especially low-frequency variants, remained undetected by existing reference panels. In the Chinese population, the TOPMed panel required an R2 threshold of 0.60-0.70 to achieve comparable imputation accuracy of the ChinaMAP panel without R2 filtering, challenging the standard practice of applying a fixed R2 threshold for downstream analyses. Regional analysis highlighted the role of recent selection in imputation discrepancies and revealed an enrichment of immune-related genes in poorly imputed regions. In addition, we showed that the selection of reference panels and R2 thresholds could significantly influence estimation of polygenic risk score for disease prediction. These findings underscore the importance of developing ancestrally diverse reference panels and provide valuable guidelines for improving genotype imputation in East and Southeast Asian populations.

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is a rapid, multi-omics technique that has revolutionized our understanding of the transcriptome at the cellular level, yet data integration remains a major challenge. To facilitate accurate, smooth-running scRNA-seq models, the integration of bulk RNA sequencing (b-RRA) and single-cell RNA analysis requires robust, data integration pipelines. However, existing pipelines have high requirements for compute resources, lengthy timelines, and the abundance of data is often an obstacle. In this work, we propose a RESTful workbench for on-premise installation of cloud-based ScRNA-seq pipelines, accommodating up to 150 agents and enabling seamless interaction between the public cloud and a large number of local agents via RabbitMQ and MQTT for communication. Our repository houses a 2.0.1 version of our python scRNA-seq workbench, namely Homebrew-runs-wg20 (v0.5.0, which was trained by the Glasgow LBSRD graduate students). Our tool can be set up on any Linux machine with the required capabilities, without sophisticated knowledge of programming languages. After training by the Glasgow team, the program is highly customizable for different analytical needs. It contains a selection of tools such as Glade, BigBrain, StereoCount, Microbiome in a glass, VOC, and different classification and normalization pipelines such as Octrain, FineTrain, NetProfiler, 10G10, and 10K100k. Our workbench allows for direct user interaction with the core pipeline through the well-documented RESTful API, in addition to automated mappings between payloads and their respective programs/algorithms. Additionally, through OpenAire, and specific access to our repository, our workbench allows for in-depth web analysis of our data, in particular for the pre-clustering pipeline. Within an hour, we show that we can detect all known isoforms of GfK and find the largest isoforms at different tissue levels in multiple tissues. We also map to GfK in blood cells, CNS, and fibroblasts. We demonstrate that BioProject, Panopto, and biomescript data can be mapped and automatically curated.

By presenting the installation and straightforward configuration workflow, our pipeline on machine learning, fluid transport, and protein mapping with WebAssembly provides a vision to integrate the scRNA-seq workflow for prospective low-resource scientific applications.

Recently, the study of exoproteomes has flourished to broaden our knowledge about the biological functions of plant proteins, and in particular, the role of cell and tissue-resident chloroplast proteins, also known as cyanidome. However, accurate characterization of protein identity is usually needed for this complex proteome, as cyanidomes are typically not always composed of protein complexes but may be concentrated on a few proteins. Here, we present C6M, a platform for predicting m/transcriptional levels and protein complexes from plant thermogenomic datasets, using just five transcript features. We found that C6M could overcome the limitation of recent approaches in deconvolution of transcription start sites (TSS) and predict putative mRNA levels with about 98% prediction accuracy. C6M is available at https://github.com/solanobio/C6M/tree/master.

Template-based annotation workflows can produce substantial amounts of annotation quality if linked to a high-throughput deep learning algorithm to provide sequence-based queries. However, the annotations generated by these approaches are often too sparse to properly interpret and integrate.

Here, we describe Annotd, a deep learning-based fast RNS 1ST targeting library refinement tool that streamlines the annotation workflow. Annotd is an open-source and free software for protein domain enrichment from NGS data, specifically from the Massively Parallel Sequencing (MPS) platforms from Thermo Fisher and Illumina. We combine AnnotationProcessor, a state-of-the-art low-resource RNA secondary structure prediction tool based on denoising unsupervised variant discovery and structural analyses for sequence quality checking, with RAnaconda, a machine learning (ML) reference library and methods with a focus on accuracy, reliability and speed, and published alongside Annotd. Annotd is used with Annotater, a workflow that allows annotators to generate rich, compact, high-resolution annotations. Annotd was launched on February 14th, 2021. Annotater is available here.

Transcriptome sequencing data generated by high-throughput sequencing technologies are now broadly available in the open access with no cost to gene annotation and visualization, which are thus being used as potential sources of new model organisms for resource genomics, in particular to facilitate functional and evolutionary characterization. However, high-throughput data also often requires post-processing to increase the level of data reproducibility across different research groups or laboratories. In this study we aimed to assess an in-house pipeline that uses the open-source software TopTools for transcriptome quality control and analyze gene ontology (GO) terms from UCSC Encyclopedia of Life (EOL) based on the NCBI RefSeq project. We assessed the stability of our results by cross-validation for comparisons with previously generated high-throughput data and on comparison with other gene annotations in the literature, by means of supervised, supervised, and unsupervised learning. Results show that our initial pipeline, including "TopTools-Ensembl" and "Aka44" annotations and features, results in very consistent results as compared to the original features from MetaboThemes using XLweb as transcriptomic annotation database, as well as similar to other publicly available transcriptomic assemblies. Using supervised learning approach, we detect aberrant gene annotation levels commonly found in RNA-sequencing reads, such as false transcription. Though they represent a distinct feature, we also use unsupervised learning technique to detect patterns of noise that usually tend to come from transcript assembly and/or gene prediction error, respectively. Moreover, we evaluate features that are not necessarily useful from a computational genomics perspective. The median value for the top-three features used for supervised learning approaches is 0.02, lower than other public annotated genes. Beyond that, we observe that the features overlap more commonly between Ensembl and annotations, but sometimes are not highly informative. For instance, features that tend to coincide, have no meaning from a gene annotation perspective.

Comparative quantitative proteomics reveals a multitude of structural proteome assemblies from diverse cell types, which were not accounted for by the current genetic model. Conversely, the literature considers recent classical methods, which focus on learning broad protein and pseudogenomic classifiers from multiple laboratories with disparate data, to be limited. We develop an extended probabilistic learning framework, for unbiased representation learning of the proteome from any dataset. Our network model of protein dynamics in cells correlates structure with function, and enables the representation of source collections with a corresponding comparison matrix and a network representation with networks. The scoring function incorporates several types of comparison, such as positional, scaffold-fold-credit, effector-effector relationship, and energy, while accounting for failure, multiple fingerprints, false negatives, and positive doubling events. The model achieves accurate classification of primitive structures (protein kinase domain, transmembrane region, signal recognition particle), with most of the structures classified successfully by 95%. The function accurately distinguishes functional species from pseudogenomic species, by 97%, with most of the structures classified successfully by 85%. We found that though the network model accounts for diverse datasets, it remains imprecise in comparison with sources containing few structures.

Key methodological contributions include: (i) we create the Atlas of Protein Identifiers and Protein Associations (APPA), an interspecies proteome reference database; (ii) we apply the extended non-negative matrix factorization (XNMF) to overcome known challenges for large-scale comparative proteomics; (iii) we provide a modular approach to organize and store comparative and experimental data; and (iv) we estimate construction costs associated with different data structures. Our findings demonstrate the utility of the extended probabilistic learning framework for comparative proteomic research, providing the necessary groundwork to more accurately analyze the proteome.

Illumina TRump-Seq, in its many uses, relies on the optimization of specific steps of the process, mostly at the level of end-to-end design of suitable algorithms. The next challenge of this pipeline is to understand the contribution and optimization of each implemented step, as well as the performance and robustness in the sense of overall scalability. We present this work by compiling a workflow for mRNA-Seq differential analysis and deconvolution. For each transcript, we start with an initial dataset that includes a representative subset of annotated features from diverse biological pipelines (Cellranger, Tophat2, Decipher, Starfile, STAR-seq, gene transcription calculation, etc.). First, we tune the process in order to maximize the performance for the given predictions. After that, we implement several regression-based approaches (e.g., Fisher M, GeneRank, Decision Trees, etc.) to adjust the number of genes detected. Then, we compare the performance of these methods in terms of false-positive, false-negative, detection rate, nucleotide noise, and entropy. The tuning results in a substantial increase in performance of the framework, especially considering the accessibility and usage of existing algorithms and implementations as suitable tools for further development. In the end, we combine these results, extending the training data representation to any well-designed DNA-Seq pipeline. We also demonstrate some robustness and performance in the process with statistically powerful tools. This is done by using the same dataset as the original template, and it allows us to perform gene prediction experiments for each gene individually, and to test the stability and robustness of the genes identification after an additional layer of filtering. Our extensive work enables us to show how to improve the robustness and accuracy of algorithms to achieve the highest possible performance while tuning, particularly in light of the increase in data diversity and the evolution of other mechanisms for the prediction of molecular bases.

Here we demonstrate high-throughput transcriptomics data acquisition, annotation, and analysis from frozen DNA in a 40-micrometer DNA block. Our platform drastically decreases the dependency of classical RNA labeling libraries and improves target specificity. Our design enables different flow-through mass cytometry methods, as well as sample preparation to meet the complex needs of mass spectrometry experiments. Our approach is also straightforward to use on PC (Macs) cells, without the need for DNA shearing or ultrastructural post-PCR purification for clone recovery.

HighlightsProteogenomic studies performed without or with sample preparation, can be carried out within 6 hours

Same day frozen/blotted samples analyzed by flow-through mass cytometry, expanding sample pipeline to 30 days

Simple workflow with our Flow-Through Mass Cytometry approach in tissue slices

Simplified sample preparation increases ease and speed, while optimized lysis allows for higher metabolite purity from the target samples.

We propose BioCLIMAT 3D FlowFACS, a computational approach to automatically generate a 3D genome assembly, guided by detailed information from an RNA-Seq trajectory that defines the time points of genomics reading frames and the resulting bioinformatic structure (seqID, AF, stretch, RBA, and FETA class). We used reference RNA sequence reads from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and C. elegans imaginal discs, which are in the primary site for imprinted gene silencing. Using BioCLIMAT as input, the developed pipeline successfully generated a highly accurate genome in less than 2 days and annotated each read with the correct bioinformatic topology. All annotations were placed in the correct biological location (transcriptome/genomics) and refined to a high level of accuracy. Compared to manual annotation, BioCLIMAT’s genome assembly was ~17-fold faster in terms of time to annotate for manual annotation, with a mean quality-based accuracy of ~99% at both DNA and RNA sequences. The model was validated with four independent genomes, including a Pac Bio experiment.

While large genomic datasets provide a powerful platform for genomic structure analysis, achieving high efficiency and superior resolution in individual-level genomic datasets remains a long-standing challenge. In this study, we present ShimmOS, an approach to asynchronously monitor non-local transcription across an entire genome, producing genetically labelled read-based profiles at a single resolution. By making the genotype explicit in a label-free manner, we identify all isoforms of proteins with high confidence, revealing hidden isoform clusters that are not necessarily observed across the same gene and allowing offline transcript quantification. We demonstrate the accuracy and reliability of our approach by outperforming established deep sequencing and transcriptomics approaches. We further investigate the reliability of our method to reveal and quantify isoform clusters of amino acid sequences without knowledge of their order in the transcriptome. Finally, we show that ancient exomes and insomes can be identified, aligning genomes with different genome annotations and estimating ancient allele frequencies. Our findings highlight the broad potential of multiplexed near-individual high-throughput methods to support transcriptomics discovery across an entire genome, while enabling real-time monitoring of isoform expression and local changes of transcript expression.

This study introduces the BNAMEproteinset and utilizes its multiple alignments to streamline the pipeline for aligning gene-expression data for high-resolution sub-cellular phenotypes. The BNAMEset serves as a common standardized folder of gene promoters, annotated gene annotations, gene lengths, microRNAs, and more. The resulting raw datasets include 437 proteins from over 20,000 experiments. The pipeline leverages simple algorithms that help align isoforms, construct stable chimeric transcripts, and produce gene expression matrices. It provides the following options: selecting one of 5000 "bowtie" aligned protein isoforms, BLAST-search for non-bowtie aligned isoforms, or optional clustering to further distil the results. Moreover, the pipeline generates novel isoforms, which include spanning open reading frames (ORFs), transcriptional regulators, and transcriptional repressors. The resulting readouts offer researchers the opportunity to compare gene expression in multiple contexts to make crucial inferences in genomic and gene activation programs.
sample_p_texts: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) has long been a cornerstone in dimensionality reduction for high-dimensional data, including single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). However, PCAs performance typically degrades with increasing data size, can be sensitive to outliers, and assumes linearity. Recently, Random Projection (RP) methods have emerged as promising alternatives, addressing some of these limitations. This study systematically and comprehensively evaluates PCA and RP approaches, including Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and randomized SVD, alongside Sparse and Gaussian Random Projection algorithms, with a focus on computational efficiency and downstream analysis effectiveness. We benchmark performance using multiple scRNA-seq datasets including labeled and unlabeled publicly available datasets. We apply Hierarchical Clustering and Spherical K-Means clustering algorithms to assess downstream clustering quality. For labeled datasets, clustering accuracy is measured using the Hungarian algorithm and Mutual Information. For unlabeled datasets, the Dunn Index and Gap Statistic capture cluster separation. Across both dataset types, the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) metric is used to assess variability. Additionally, locality preservation is examined, with RP outperforming PCA in several of the evaluated metrics. Our results demonstrate that RP not only surpasses PCA in computational speed but also rivals and, in some cases, exceeds PCA in preserving data variability and clustering quality. By providing a thorough benchmarking of PCA and RP methods, this work offers valuable insights into selecting optimal dimensionality reduction techniques, balancing computational performance, scalability, and the quality of downstream analyses.

MotivationDe novo genes emerge from previously non-coding regions of the genome, challenging the traditional view that new genes primarily arise through duplication and adaptation of existing ones. Characterised by their rapid evolution and their novel structural properties or functional roles, de novo genes represent a young area of research. Therefore, the field currently lacks established standards and methodologies, leading to inconsistent terminology and challenges in comparing and reproducing results.

ResultsThis work presents a standardised annotation format to document the methodology of de novo gene datasets in a reproducible way. We developed DeNoFo, a toolkit to provide easy access to this format that simplifies annotation of datasets and facilitates comparison across studies. Unifying the different protocols and methods in one standardised format, while providing integration into established file formats, such as fasta or gff, ensures comparability of studies and advances new insights in this rapidly evolving field.

Availability and ImplementationDeNoFo is available through the official Python Package Index (PyPI) and at https://github.com/EDohmen/denofo. All tools have a graphical user interface and a command line interface. The toolkit is implemented in Python3, available for all major platforms and installable with pip and uv.

Compositional data analysis (CoDA) is an emerging statistical framework and has been extended to microbiome, bulk RNA-seq, and cell type proportions in single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) (with 50-200 components). Here, we explore the high-dimensional application of CoDA (CoDA-hd) and its various log-ratio (LR) transformations to raw count matrices of scRNA-seq which has over 20,000 components (e.g., protein coding genes). scRNA-seq matrices are typically sparse and high-dimensional. Common approaches of normalization such as log-normalization may lead to suspicious findings as previously shown for trajectory inference. Although RNA-seq is compositional data by nature, the geometry of CoDA in high-dimensional simplex is not compatible with most downstream analyses of scRNA-seq which are based on Euclidean space. In this study, we explored if CoDA is adaptable with scRNA-seq in various downstream applications. Specifically, we attempted to study: (1) CoDA adaptability to scRNA-seq; (2) handling of zero data: prior-log-normalized, imputation or with specific count addition; (3) transformation to Euclidean space and compatibility with downstream analyses. Our results suggested that (1) the innovative count addition schemes (e.g., SGM) enable the application of CoDA to high dimensional sparse data (i.e., scRNA-seq); (2) log-normalized data could be transformed to CoDA LR transformation as an approximation; (3) CoDA LR transformations such as count-added centered-log-ratio (CLR) had some advantages in dimension reduction visualization, clustering, and trajectory inference in the tested real & simulated datasets. CLR provided more decent and separated clusters in dimension reductions, improved the Slingshot trajectory inference, and eliminated the suspicious trajectory that is probably caused by the dropouts. We therefore concluded that CoDA may be a preferred scale-free model to handle scRNA-seq data for these downstream applications. Additionally, an R package  CoDAhd was developed for conducting CoDA LR transformations for high dimensional scRNA-seq data. The code for implementing CoDA-hd and some example datasets were placed at https://github.com/GO3295/CoDAhd.

Interpreting the vast amounts of data generated by high-throughput sequencing technologies can often present a significant challenge, particularly for non-model organism. While automated approaches like GO (Gene Ontology) and KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) enrichment analyses are widely used, they often lack specificity for non-model organisms. To bridge this gap, we present a manually curated gene list tailored for teleost fish transcriptomics. This resource focuses on key biological processes crucial for understanding teleost fish physiology, development, and adaptation, including hormone signaling, various metabolic pathways, appetite regulation, digestion, gastrointestinal function, vision, ossification, osmoregulation, and pigmentation. Developed through collaborative efforts of specialists in diverse fields, the list prioritizes genes with established roles in teleost physiology, experimental evidence, and conservation across species. This curated list aims to provide researchers with a reliable starting point for transcriptomic analyses, offering a carefully evaluated set of genes relevant to current research priorities. By streamlining the process of gene selection and interpretation, this resource supports the broader teleost fish research community in designing and analyzing studies that investigate molecular responses to developmental and environmental changes. We encourage the scientific community to collaboratively expand and refine this list, ensuring its continued relevance and utility for teleost fish research.

BackgroundDetecting protein-coding genes in nucleotide sequences is a significant challenge for understanding genome and transcriptome function, yet the reliability of bioinformatic tools for this task remains largely unverified. This is despite some tools being available for several decades, and widely used for genome and transcriptome annotation.

ResultsWe perform an assessment of nucleotide sequence and alignment-based de novo protein-coding detection tools. The controls we use exclude any previous training dataset and include coding exons as a positive set and length-matched intergenic and shuffled sequences as negative sets.

Our work demonstrates that several widely used tools are neither accurate nor computationally efficient for the protein-coding sequence detection problem. In fact, just three of nine tools significantly outperformed a naive scoring scheme. Furthermore, we note a high discrepancy between self-reported accuracies and the accuracy achieved in our study. Our results show that the extra dimension from conserved and variable nucleotides in alignments have a significant advantage over single sequence approaches.

ConclusionsThese results highlight significant limitations in existing protein-coding annotation tools that are widely used for lncRNA annotation. This shows a need for more robust and efficient approaches to training and assessing the performance of tools for identifying protein-coding sequences. Our study paves the way for future advancements in comparative genomic approaches, and we hope will popularise more robust approaches to genome and transcriptome annotation.

Seeing is believing. Visualizing Ribo-seq and other sequencing data within genes of interest is a powerful approach to studying gene expression, but its application is limited by a lack of robust tools. Here, we introduce ggRibo, a user-friendly R package for visualizing individual gene expression, integrating Ribo-seq, RNA-seq, and other genome-wide datasets with flexible scaling options. ggRibo visualizes 3-nucleotide periodicity, a hallmark of translating ribosomes, within a gene-structure context, including introns and untranslated regions, enabling the study of novel ORFs, translation of different isoforms, and mechanisms of translational regulation. ggRibo can plot multiple Ribo-seq/RNA-seq datasets from different conditions for comparison. It also contains functions for plotting single-transcript view, reading-frame decomposition, and RNA-seq coverage alone. Importantly, ggRibo supports the visualization of other omics datasets that could also be presented with single-nucleotide resolution, such as RNA degradome, transcription start sites, translation initiation sites, and epitranscriptomic modifications. We demonstrate its utility with examples of upstream ORFs, downstream ORFs, nested ORFs, and differential isoform translation in humans, Arabidopsis, tomato, and rice. We also provide examples of multi-omic comparisons that reveal insights that connect the transcriptome, translatome, and degradome. In summary, ggRibo is an advanced single-gene viewer that offers a valuable resource for studying gene expression regulation through its intuitive and flexible platform.

The transcriptome encompasses all RNA transcripts in eukaryotic cells, orchestrating gene expression and regulating cellular function, development, and adaptation. Identifying open reading frames (ORFs) in transcripts is a critical step in transcriptome analysis. We introduce TD2, a new tool for ab initio annotation of protein-coding ORFs in transcripts. We find TD2 to be sensitive and precise when compared to other state-of-the-art tools in reference transcripts and transcriptome assemblies from a diverse array of eukaryotes.

TD2 is available at https://github.com/Markusjsommer/TD2. The project is open-source, developed in Python with PyTorch, and is freely available to all academic, government, and commercial users under the MIT license.

sample_q_texts: Eversion of multiple sensory pathways can accompany dysfunctions of the peripheral visual pathway (PV). In the cerebellar peduncles (CPs), aberrant bipolar neurons in visual pathways may control gaze and vestibular integration. However, the regulation of corticospinal excitability during cerebellar Eversion has not been identified. Therefore, using non-human primates to delineate corticospinal function, we designed, carried out, and statistically modeled Eversion-associated oscillations. We applied confocal MRI, electroencephalography, and optogenetic experiments to elucidate how bipolar neurons in CPs influence Cortical excitability. Direct observations of neospinocerebellar circuitry in humans with corticospinal suppression are particularly challenging due to the monosynaptic nature of MSIs, which likely represent Eversion. We found that Eversion alters the modulation of the lateral corticospinal pathway (LCS), contrasting with IPSP recorded in CP slices. The CSIS reduction is mirrored by LCES lowering. These findings highlight the importance of motor evoked potentials and corticospinal mechanisms as controlling the modulatory state of vestibular cortex. Interestingly, LCE modulated by S-13 is insensitive to CSIS and Eversion, likely due to the strong concurrent influence of half-amplitude imaging, which could modulate these pathways through competing interoceptive neural circuits.

Clever neurons promote neuron-to-signalling pathways within the cognitive motor cortex. Cholinergic neurons are thought to mediate those mechanisms, but they are likely silent at relaxed firing rates. Here we use a visible 3D dynamic light-sheet imaging panel in mice (SynIC panels) to test the hypothesis that cholinergic synapses mediate striatum-to-cortical signalling in the neocortex as well as its motor circuits. Striatal cholinergic neurons are co-released with corticosterone in response to stimulus, but the physiological mechanisms and functional consequences of corticosterone in the neocortex are unknown. We show that spontaneous currents in the cholinergic interneurons in the subthalamic (StiSti) and nigral (StiNig) control of motion in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) are sensitive to corticosterone. Comparing 3D visual patterns recorded in the upper parietal brainstem with mPFC high-frequency (64 Hz) and low-frequency (50 Hz) sliding field in rodents, we uncovered that low frequency fields did not generate the same amplitudes of co-release of Cholinergic neurotransmitters as do high frequency fields. This provides an explanation for previously unidentified neuronal mechanisms mediating cholinergic interneurons motion.

There is an extensive literature connecting neuroplasticity, adaptation, and the cognitive and behavioral manifestations of schizophrenia. Neuroimaging studies have identified increased parietal- and occipital-prefrontal cortical activity in schizophrenia. Different theoretical frameworks have been proposed to explain this pattern: namely, decreased excitatory activity (e.g., dysfunction or increase in glutamate) and enhanced inhibitory activity (e.g., reduction in the degree of hippocampal-subiculum input to various parietal and frontal cortex substrates). However, little is known about the neuroplasticity underlying this observation. The first line of investigation is qualitative, however; methods to identify spatially distinct regions and their correlates are lacking. We developed a robust machine learning algorithm for identifying gamma-frequency in brain maps derived from functional neuroimaging data. We detected gamma-frequency in occipital and parietal prefrontal cortex in schizophrenia. Even more importantly, we identified regions in prefrontal and parietal precentral cortex that may be functionally involved in modulating gamma-frequency in schizophrenia. We postulate that such interactionally-constrained gamma waves are due to modulation by the prefrontal lobes, influenced by dorsal anterior cingulate, but not anterior insula, and possibly augmented by precentral cortex. Conversely, our statistical model revealed that the precentral cortex strongly interacts with the occipital cortex; the precentral-occipital intermodular interaction constrains the connection between each hemisphere of the precentral cortex and each central or subcortical inferior parietal lobe. Together, these findings demonstrate our method for identifying a specific role for intermodular interactions and particular molecular correlates of the interplay between lateral-lobe structures.

The human brain is remarkably diverse and responsive to environmental stimulation, with substantial age-related alterations, albeit there remains a paucity of studies investigating the effects of neurostimulation in the first year of life. The exploration of reward-guided learning in infancy is limited. Thus, our study aims to investigate if the distribution of neonatal eyeblink social eye-movements, assessing the impact of visually engaging orientation sessions in an olfactory-negative habituation paradigm, can predict visual-motor function in the first year of life. In a sample of 21 babies aged 3-22 months, videos of an ambiguous face, with slight variations in proportion of unpredicted object size on the face, were presented to participants, and the object was presented subsequently with an auditory tone. The onset of the first eyeblink was synchronised with the beginning of the auditory auditory sound. Training baseline eyeblink duration was of 30 ms. The habituation task consisted of three sessions lasting 1 min each with five 500 ms sequence shifts, alternating between visual (V) and auditory stimuli, and lasted a total of 20 min. Participants were classified into 2 groups: V+A (8 V+A trials) and V+A+O (4 V+A trials with 4 A trials): N1, N2, N3 and subsequent visual attention. Results demonstrate a significant effect of age in eyeblink observation when V+A was played with stimuli of short duration, with a positive impact on HR and BB. Moreover, our results demonstrate age effects on fatigue in V+A+O and in V+A (p<0.05). Our results showed that both the O+A condition and the V+A+O condition were ineffective in the V+O sample.

The reciprocal inhibitory (RI) modulation mechanism depends on the coordinated action of several neurotransmitter systems. In cerebellar granule cells, GAD67-immunolabeling (GLI-IC) and GABA1a-subunit coexpression are associated with MI, while no correlation with the effect of NMDA-receptor dysfunction (NoE) is observed. We set out to explore the role of these components of the MI circuit in the unique role that regular activities of the cerebellum play in sensory processing. Using stimulation, we found that a single burst of noise-sensitive activity can enhance cerebellar MI by a factor of ~10 on a motion-sensory grid produced with an ultrashort, short-duration, or long-duration stimulator. Besides, in the human Myoclonus Model (MMM) mice that lack excitatory NMDA receptor subunits and, concomitantly, are devoid of recumbency inhibition in the MI circuit, motor excitability is highly affected by repeated noise-sensory activity-induced MI (F(I/F(N) NE / "0.5 / "0.5). However, these excitability effects were absent in human Ross babies and in MMMM mice subjected to repetitive stimulation only. We conclude that regular spontaneous activities of the cerebellar MI circuit contribute to the specific role that regular activities of the cerebellum play in motor control of visual-gaze maintenance.

ImportanceWhereas MI plays a major role in interneurons, the function of MI in interneurons exhibiting excitation-disinhibited and arousal-impaired (i.e., "sensory") states is poorly understood. In addition to visual systems, sensory-motor interactions of this type are crucial for normal brain function. Here, using a noise-transient model with recurrent synaptic transmission, we demonstrate that exposure to continuous noise-induced sensory-motor communication circuits further recruits recurrent excitation-disinhibited activity to ME inhibition.

Natural senile tremor (SST), a relatively infrequent neurological condition, arises as a result of aging, marked by an increase in neuronal and synaptic reserve. These changes affect cortical excitability, neuronal firing frequency and system connectivity, but the underlying mechanisms are currently poorly defined. Here, we studied sensory input responses using whole-body whole-excitability in nine people with natural, cortical-like self-moving tremor (NMLST), and nine with classical catatonia (Cat). We applied functional neuroimaging to whole-brain responses to sensory stimuli in the motor and visual cortex areas (3A, 3D, 3F and 5F respectively). SST and Cat participants showed varying degrees of insensitivity to vestibular, visual, or both aversive and proprioceptive inputs. Moreover, SST showed widespread decreases in ventral and/or dorsal portions of the frontal lobe. Only a subset of Cat participants showed normal projections. We also discovered a subpopulation of Cat participants with a strong blood-brain barrier (BBB) and normalized GABAergic synaptic connections with the ventral corticostriatal and brainstem. Further studies are required to pinpoint the exact mechanisms of SSTAx's pathogenetic mechanisms and to explore neurophysiologically-based biomarkers that might enable early diagnosis.

Convex animals use a modulation of propagation dynamics and neural spike timing for high-level information processing, not by means of spike-timing-dependent plasticity but by releasing positive preattentive selective attention. Recent findings from neuroscience suggest that waves of neural activity (representing neural populations) could convey different kinds of information. Meanwhile, interference noise might cause a build-up of beta waves and an inhibition of high-level activities in the brain. We reasoned that high-level information could be manifested by a reduction of activity, by reduced positive pre-activated alpha activity, and by stimulated inhibition in neural oscillations. We predicted that high-frequency beta waves could trigger a self-reinforcing modulation of neural activity from alpha and delta populations and reduce neural signals, while a beta rise in the sensory processing network could exert a selective release in the population of excitable cells from the visual systems. One study showed a dose-dependent reduction of alpha-frequency oscillations in the inferior occipital lobe, a parietal visual cortico-cortical cortical projection, and a parietal retinotopic visual field of human subjects. The reduction in excitation was most pronounced in contralateral visual field projections and was blocked by simultaneous application of the antagonist response of a calcium channel blocker. The second study in humans applied a virtual reality to suppress specific temporal and frequency-domain features of gamma frequency in occipital cortex, a parietal visual field, and parietal visual cortical projections, as well as a cortical projection with parietal views of objects and their outlines on two orthogonal display planes. Application of the antagonist also blocked the deleterious effects of gamma frequency suppression on alpha frequency in the parietal visual field. Our proposal is that executive attention could manifest in the suppression of cortical and thalamic gamma frequency in the visual system, and in reduced gamma frequency in brain regions projecting into the visual system.

In motor control, interhemispheric brain asymmetry affects both motor behavior and underlying neuronal circuits. Conversely, deviations from the mean motor-system transmission pattern are apparent in stroke and various forms of cognitive dysfunctions. Spatial "super-différance" is a neuroplastic reorganization principle that leads to less effective corticofugal transmission to non-dominant cortical regions and represents one of the key features of motor and cognitive impairments. Although asymmetry and super-différence typically manifest only across hemifields, the role of brain asymmetry-dependent effects on the distribution of mesial temporal structures (MTs) remains unclear. Here, we show that MS-associated, cortically controlled spontaneous motor behavior is maintained in mice with unilaterally constricted MTs, a state in which cognitive function including spatial working memory is impaired. We demonstrate that this effect is maintained, along with the absence of cortical asymmetry, in parallel control and wild-type mice while demonstrating that this effect persists across the MT constriction. Together, these results demonstrate that the selective modulation of single neurons in terms of MT segmentation can be maintained across cortex despite the loss of cortical asymmetry.

The Cerebellar Magnetoencephalography project aims to learn about motor learning processes by measuring the human response to headmovement perturbations induced in a voxel-by-voxel fashion. In this talk we describe the setup of the sensors, the features included in the microchip, and details of the sensor design. In addition, we describe how sensor outputs are translated into predictive cortical models that can reproduce various motor motor task performance. Models such as the badr algorithm have been widely used in the literature for estimating predictive models for motor tasks. Many advanced models of motion based on the Hierarchical Bayesian approach have been able to increase the goodness of fit. These models are built within the Viterbi algorithm. Model agnostic and generative methods may be used to further enhance predictive performance. In this work, we focus on the latter through the adaptation of the deconvolution step, allowing us to anticipate, evaluate, and compare various prediction models. A brief review of the 3-layer unsupervised gradient descent neural network is also presented, incorporating a novel technique for the addition of a self-learning component. This component allows for the realization of models in which self-learning is at the heart of an algorithm and can be applied independently.

This research uncovers a novel psychological mechanism for suppressing visual information processing in normal aging. Whereas the role of BOLD-MR imaging activity is unquestionable, the role of encoding and response to the resulting excitatory network is surprisingly inconclusive. Flocculent inverse dynamics of firing rates for multiphoton glutamate-N3 (mGluN3) is investigated as a signpost of uninhibited excitatory activity as the condition under investigation. Analysis of the 51m-T1C-TAM-effect following mGluN3 stimulation in healthy individuals suggests that corticospinal mGluN3 depolarizes presynaptic mGluN3 sites (at the spine of M1 region; 22 synaptic sites) in the long-loop-area of the M1 region, resulting in a suppression of gamma activity. These findings are accompanied by a decrease of mGluN3-containing dendrites in the mGluN3 (at spine) voxels and an increase of dopsin-containing dendrites (at spine) voxels within the dopsin-2 (Dop-2) nucleus. Thus, functional and structural difference between presynaptic and postsynaptic mGluN3 dendrites emerges. Reversal of the inhibitory effects of gamma-mGluN3 upon mouse cingulate cortex stimulation suggests a "negative" mechanism, which remains hidden for long time because it is mediated by a long-distance inhibitory wave. This results in a "global" dissociation of the high-frequency delayed gamma-dopamine, as evidenced by the comparison with reduced ECoG activity in Delta delta-monkeys. This activation of presynaptic mGluN3-expressing mGluN3 dendrites is associated with the "global" dissociation of gamma-D-alpha motor signals: High-frequency in-trajectory gamma-D-alpha activation in the hippocampus and corticolimbic pathways but, in contrast, a suppression of high-frequency d-alpha in the extralimbic corticolimbic as well as in the parieto-subcortical pathway (PST).
