sample_p_texts: Characterizing the early development of the human brain is critical from both fundamental and clinical perspectives. However, existing neuroimaging techniques are either not well suited to infants or have limited spatial or temporal resolution. The advent of optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) has revolutionized magnetoencephalography (MEG) by enabling wearable and thus more naturalistic recordings while maintaining excellent sensitivity and spatiotemporal resolution. Nevertheless, its adaptation to studying neural activity in infancy poses several challenges. In this work, we present an original close-to-scalp OPM-MEG setup that successfully recorded brain responses to sounds in newborns. We exposed one-month-old infants to continuous streams of tones and observed significant evoked responses, which peaked [~]250 ms poststimulus at bilateral auditory cortices. When tones were presented at a steady fixed pace with an oddball tone every fourth tone, significant neural responses were found both at the frequency of the standard tones (3 Hz) and of the oddball tones (0.75 Hz). The latter reflects the ability of the newborn brain to detect auditory change and synchronize to regular auditory patterns. Additional analyses support the added value of triaxial OPMs to increase the number of channels on small heads. Finally, OPM-MEG responses were validated with those obtained from the same participants using an adult-sized cryogenic MEG. This study demonstrates the applicability of OPM-MEG to study early postnatal periods; a crucial step towards future OPM investigations of typical and pathological early brain development.

Some of the most dramatic examples of neuroplasticity in the human brain follow congenital sensory deprivation, though we have limited understanding of the plasticity mechanisms driving such large-scale remapping. Hand loss due to congenital limb differences (CLD) offers a unique temporal dissociation of developmental neuroplasticity mechanisms: While sensory deprivation is congenital, compensatory motor behaviours develop progressively across childhood. Using paediatric neuroimaging and semi-ecological behavioural analysis in children (5-7 years old) and adults (>25 years old) with unilateral upper-limb CLD, we studied deprivation- and use-dependent plasticity in the deprived primary somatosensory cortex and beyond. We reveal that global remapping, encompassing the entire sensory homunculus, is established early and maintained in adulthood. We demonstrate that deprivation-driven homeostatic plasticity can drive this global remapping, with Hebbian-based compensatory learning further contributing to inter-individual differences both in childhood and adulthood. Our findings emphasise the early establishment and stability of cortical maps, despite extensive daily-life behavioural adaptation.

Disruption of the balance between excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission (E-I balance) underlies theories of many neurodevelopmental disorders, however, its study is typically restricted to adults, animal models and the lab-bench. Neurophysiological oscillations in the gamma frequency band relate closely to E-I balance, and a new technology - OPM-MEG - offers the possibility to measure such signals across the lifespan. We used OPM-MEG to measure gamma oscillations induced by visual stimulation in >100 participants, aged 2-34 years. We demonstrate a significantly changing spectrum with age, with low amplitude broadband gamma oscillations in children and high amplitude band limited oscillations dominating in adults. We used a canonical cortical microcircuit to model these gamma signals, revealing significant age-related shifts in E-I balance in superficial pyramidal neurons in visual cortex. Our findings detail the first MEG metrics of gamma oscillations and their underlying generators from toddlerhood, providing a benchmark against which future studies can contextualise.

sample_q_texts: Previously, we developed a method to generate optimized sequence-level protein models from literature data by adapting motif search (MTS) techniques to the problems of protein modeling. This approach has been applied to almost 400 models of single-domain proteins and has shown significant acceleration in terms of feasibility and quality of the models, according to a comprehensive evaluation done at our institution using MockDF. However, this approach relies solely on known, text-based protein sequences as input. A critical challenge in using them is that the input sequence was preprocessed and linearized, which impacted model performance. During this preprocessing, non-translated amino acids are removed in most cases due to quality-assessing purposes. Additionally, a large number of variables, such as ion charge and ligand binding modes, are determined prior to the training of the initial latent space of the Gaussian process model, which necessitates a thorough setup of the training data. On the other hand, our method avoids these preprocessing steps, leveraging preexisting dictionaries and text mining, and also in some cases utilizing protein structures themselves. Despite having a higher level of success with the masked Gaussian process models, recent analysis has found variations in model performance, often observed at moderate levels of similarity between input sequences. A qualitative statistical analysis carried out shows that models optimized for sequences shorter than, but generally not wider than, the accuracy threshold, were more prone to model overfitting. This study evaluates the results of using different training and validation data sets.

To help clinicians and clinicians working with model predictions in their daily clinical practice to identify and isolate critical decisions in the future, we have developed predictive workflows, called Metabolic Training Sets (MTSs), that integrate different computational models and enable consistent comparison between models and choices. Thus, to share algorithmic adaptations from other models to potential clinical needs, a metadata-structured set of tool integration capabilities is designed and structured as MetaStrainMTSs (MTSMTSs) using SynBioML, a computational tool and framework for storing and accessing files and metadata for synthetic protein models. By analyzing the translation, data, analysis, and model steps for any hypothetical model, computational implementations and software can be identified and compared to improve the efficiency of the workflow.

Methods: We use MetaStrainMTSs (named e.g. CoQ10-MTSMTS) for the integration of an external functional assay with the in-house BiogSoftware to facilitate prediction of CoQ10 levels at subcellular localization. We perform a validation through data resampling to test the robustness of an in-house BiogSoftware as well as to show and test the differences of two structural and functional covariates in addition to the assay in a test set. To date, MTSs have been used by 190 biomedical AI researchers from 44 medical institutions. In a second round of user-driven analysis, results and tool possibilities were reviewed (in parallel) by all other 76 main users. Finally, our tool is being prepared for commercialization. To date, 38 STS have been built, with potential to be used in other program libraries. See user-studies.

A critical advantage of drug discovery is identifying critical signaling pathways. Identifying unannotated inhibitors against new drug targets is a formidable challenge to the science of program-based drug design due to limited data. There is a general lack of significant pipeline programs to compare inhibitors to their targets. Here, we developed a data-driven simulation approach, wherein we generated new targets within target domains with comparable amino acid sequences as existing targets. We demonstrated that our high-throughput program-based de novo inhibitor discovery engine does not bias towards target candidate inhibitors that already exist in the system. The predicted compounds were more similar to existing drugs and existing drug targets than to the target itself. Furthermore, the false discovery rates of the inhibitor pools were lower than 95%, demonstrating an effective approach to optimize the discovery of new drug targets. These findings pave the way for improved non-traditional high-throughput computational platform-based drug target discovery pipelines, including pipeline design tools and inhibitors.

One significant challenge in pharmaceutical discovery is establishing the physicochemical properties of uncharacterized proteins. Here, we developed the AI-powered musproffigan-based computational platform Musproffigan to assess the impact of surface and thermodynamic properties on affinity and stability for developed protein design and property characterization. Utilizing two K242E mutations for representation in molecular docking studies, Musproffigan accurately predicted 197 accessible aa sequences and the side-chain propensity of these proteins, aiding in rationalizing surface changes, such as inherent dynamic environments and extrinsic/ intrinsic adjustments in safety and potency. To validate the accuracy of musproffigan predictions, our approach was evaluated for effectiveness when evaluating five small molecule modulators of tetraspan-1 (TSPO) binding and selectivity. Using computational strategies, we assessed protein accessibility for natural and mutated ligand binding modes for the apical, distal domains, and their combinations and compared with validation assays in brain slices. Finally, we evaluated musproffigan predictions in compound screening against the global binding site of TSPO (D1493G), which demonstrated high accuracy in determining variability between individual ligands of interest in binding mode for D1493. Altogether, these results demonstrate the utility of musproffigan in addressing large-scale structural and property-related challenges in the pharmaceutical discovery pipeline of high-complexity proteins.

ObjectiveTo assess the validity of automated methods for constraining zinc finger protein (ZFP) interactions, particularly those defined using SWISS-PROT.

MethodsWe built a computational model using Swissprot to represent the ZFP and ZFP-like interactions with proteins in yeast. We tested eight methods for constraining the interaction networks in swissprot based on the evaluation on various reference crystal structures of ZFP-containing proteins, including SWISS-PROT 20201108, Fer811, and Cryo-EM structures. We used WSCJ to identify the best strategies for data integration and validation using Dynadiff and MATALIA for iterative comparison.

ResultsThe analysis of ZFP-containing protein interactions with YfjIn or T93F showed that the SWISS-PROT1 model outperformed three others including derived from traditional methods in terms of global affinity predictions. The A/B scaling approach, which incorporates structural characteristics, outperforms others in terms of the degree of biological significance of the best-results. Validation results show that a 50-nucleotide segment of H69 significantly reduces the void size of the entire ZFP domain in yeast. All the constructed crystal structures contained significant changes in backbone and loop structure.

ConclusionWe have developed a framework using WSCJ and Swissprot to assess the validity of the seven most commonly used approaches for constraining ZFP and ZFP-like interactions using publicly available comprehensive data sets. The results show that the inclusion of structural information helps correct and further model complicated spatial arrangements of proteins interacting with ZFP.

Pfam is the de facto standard for homology modeling, and its major challenge is to automatically construct protein structures from high-resolution spectroscopic data, which takes years of increasing computing power and expertise to create a comprehensive and free tool. Building on previous work, we introduce MSHAKO, a metabolic flux graph-based approach to automatically model protein structures, which greatly reduces the training effort and computational cost of building a fully functional heme metabolism model. Importantly, MSHAKO does not require or build custom software, such as specific high-performance graphics processing units, or user interaction, rather MSHAKO works directly on protein sequence databases and associated spectral data, thanks to a human-visible-interface, that allows users to interactively specify a comprehensive metabolic network that MSHAKO can then build a dynamically updated model based on the desired hierarchical taxonomic scale and modularity of the user-specified protein manifold. While MSHAKO was designed for structural descriptions, it is not limited to heme metabolism. The platform is implemented as a C++ application along with a Python interface and a REST API, making it flexible and easy to extend in future. We can leverage PIMFAST, a freely available high-throughput method to fast-build the liver proteome, to assess the performance of MSHAKO in heme metabolism models. Our extensive testbed demonstrates the utility of MSHAKO and also allows for it to be further extended in the future.

We describe here the creation of a universal (docking) tool for cell-type specific design of eukaryotic membrane proteins, which allows efficient verification of unbiased membrane docking predictions to known membrane proteins by automated detection of protein residues docked to a lipid bilayer or membrane raft of any composition. This tool is based on classical membrane folding-based docking protocols and was implemented in the bioconductor suite. To achieve the goal, the method starts from protein coding sequences associated with membrane protein design and uses it to deconstruct full membrane proteins prior to folding and docking. This allows a complete map of membrane proteins defined by the folded protein set to be generated. Then, in silico predictions for membrane proteins are categorized based on their polar-to-membrane orientation, membrane composition, lipid composition, and their spatial proximity to a membrane raft. The prediction interface allows manual selection of physicochemical or protein sequence parameters to include, with any two folding-based predictions reviewed and ranked using available literature against which the assays were performed. Proteins can also be screened in a two-time frame manner, with protein scan (screen) predictions paired with assays that assess the performance of the protein prediction algorithm. The approach has been applied to design certain membrane proteins for use in non-conventional three-dimensional membrane systems.

Target discovery (TD) is at the center of drug discovery and relies on large-scale analysis of structural data such as X-ray structures of active molecules in high-throughput simulations. Phenotype mining, as an efficient way to incorporate phenotypic data in drug discovery, can act as a target of origin to identify binding sites (TBPs) that are related to human phenotypes. However, while vast amounts of available structures are available and robust predictor models of TBPs have been developed, few have been developed for TBPs associated with human phenotypes. To develop suitable candidate models for TBPs, we propose a semi-automated method for annotating putative TBPs that correspond to a specific drug target and for using gene sets and their co-expression correlation as predictors for TBP assignment and object regression. We present in silico validation for one of the original query subject fields, protein C-terminal repeats (PTCR), both with a single cell transcriptional level and with large sample sizes. We validated this approach with data from the DrugBank Drug Targets database and with Metazoans D89 targets within a TCGA10 liver dataset. Our results show that TBPs can be identified for a range of different phenotypes using co-expression network data.

In this study, we developed an open-source Python library (PyDiph) to accurately predict protein function-signature binding to DD-Glide, a cellular protein required for Plasmodium falciparum merozoite membrane fusion, enabling predictive analysis of drug sensitivity to potential compounds that exert membrane fusion inhibition. Our platform applies De Novo sequence generation, prediction, and functional enrichment to identify all possible binding sites and test the predicted interactions with several well-validated amino acid changes using the Panther database and structural analysis of DD-Glide to predict the binding of various pharmacologically active compounds. PyDiph is now freely available at https://github.com/openmicrob/py_diph.

Chromophore-active amino acids can be identified using high-throughput NMR structure prediction techniques. However, they need to be mapped and annotated to two-dimensional structures before using these small proteins in protein interaction screens to narrow down sequence-activity pairs to the origin of the annotated mutation. This can be difficult with non-standard structures such as those in proteins with disordered regions, proteins in membrane fusion proteins, and proteins with a predicted transmembrane sequence but lacking structured residues. For these reasons, it is common to wait for mutations to be made at known crystallization or expression sites before analysis.

In this study, we have developed this task-specific optimization pipeline named Unsupervised Protein Crystal Structure (UPCS) which provides amino acid sequences with protein structures. UPCS uses the method described by Di Cicco et al. to identify native sites in the primary structure of predicted protein structures. Once the structure is completed, UPCS searches for any amino acid with N-terminal or C-terminal sequence motifs predicted to either have an amino acid counterpart in the 3D crystal structure or in a transmembrane domain. If these sequences are present in the crystal, UPCS asks the primary structure of the crystal to predict their 3D structural location. We were able to improve it significantly across the reference set.
sample_p_texts: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) are heme-containing enzymes involved in the metabolism of drugs and endogenous compounds. Humans have 57 known CYPs, with >200 mutations linked to severe disorders, highlighting their role in disease etiology. To investigate their pathogenicity, we performed an in-depth computational study, comparing pathogenic mutations with non-pathogenic ones. First, we evaluated the effects of all possible mutations across 26 known CYPs structures using five structure-and five sequence-based methods, aiming to reproduce pathogenesis. We computed 23,46,410 mutations, categorized into: all possible, non-pathogenic, and pathogenic. Comparisons consistently revealed a meaningful stability pattern: non-pathogenic > all > pathogenic. Second, we found that a significantly higher number of pathogenic mutations were buried in CYP structures, relating to their higher pathogenesis potential. Third, we analyzed mutation allele frequency relative to solvent accessibility. Fourth, we computed change in 48 amino acid properties upon mutation and identified three distinguishing features: Gibbs free energy, isoelectric point and volume. Fifth, the positive residue content was reduced significantly in diseased mutations, with arginine mutations being the main culprit, directly linked to isoelectric point change. Sixth, we found a higher propensity for pathogenic mutations in conserved sites, suggesting disruption of CYP function. Finally, analysis of heme versus substrate sites showed a higher frequency of pathogenic mutations in heme site, with arginine being the main mutating residue, possibly disrupting arginine-heme interactions. We provide the first comprehensive analysis of mutation effects across multiple CYPs. We model the chemical basis of CYP-related pathogenicity, paving way for a semi-quantitative model to predict diseases.

MotivationThe generation and analysis of diverse mutants of a protein is a powerful tool for understanding protein function. However, generating such mutants can be time-consuming, while the commercial option of buying a series of mutant plasmids can be expensive. In contrast, the insertion of a synthesized double stranded DNA (dsDNA) fragment into a plasmid is a fast and low-cost method to generate a large library of mutants with one or more point mutations, insertions, or deletions.

ResultsTo aid in the design of these DNA fragments we have developed PyVADesign: a Python package that makes the design and ordering of dsDNA fragments straight-forward and cost-effective. In PyVADesign, the mutations of interest are clustered in different cloning groups for efficient exchange into the target plasmid. Additionally, primers that prepare the target plasmid for insertion of the dsDNA fragment, as well as primers for sequencing, are automatically designed within the same program.

AvailabilityPyVADesign is open source and available at https://github.com/CDDLeiden/PyVADesign/.

Contactgerard@lacdr.leidenuniv.nl

Protein S-palmitoylation is a reversible lipophilic posttranslational modification regulating a diverse number of signaling pathways. Within transmembrane proteins (TMPs), S-palmitoylation is implicated in conditions from inflammatory disorders to respiratory viral infections. Many small-scale experiments have observed S-palmitoylation at juxtamembrane Cys residues. However, most large-scale S-palmitoyl discovery efforts rely on trypsin-based proteomics within which hydrophobic juxtamembrane regions are likely underrepresented. Machine learning- by virtue of its freedom from experimental constraints - is particularly well suited to address this discovery gap surrounding TMP S-palmitoylation. Utilizing a UniProt-derived feature set, a gradient boosted machine learning tool (TopoPalmTree) was constructed and applied to a holdout dataset of viral S-palmitoylated proteins. Upon application to the mouse TMP proteome, 1591 putative S-palmitoyl sites (i.e. not listed in SwissPalm or UniProt) were identified. Two lung-expressed S-palmitoyl candidates (synaptobrevin Vamp5 and water channel Aquaporin-5) were experimentally assessed. Finally, TopoPalmTree was used for rational design of an S-palmitoyl site on KDEL-Receptor 2. This readily interpretable model aligns the innumerable small-scale experiments observing juxtamembrane S-palmitoylation into a proteomic tool for TMP S-palmitoyl discovery and design, thus facilitating future investigations of this important modification.

The field of protein design has changed dramatically over the last 40 years, with a range of methods developing from rational design to more recent data-driven approaches. While considerable insight could be gained from analysing designed proteins, there is no single resource that brings together all the relevant data, making it difficult to identify current challenges and opportunities within the field.

Here we present the Protein Design Archive, a website and database of designed proteins. Using the database, we performed systematic analysis that reveals a rapid increase in the number and complexity of designs over time and uncovers biases in their amino-acid usage and secondary structure content. Finally, sequence- and structure-based analysis demonstrates the breadth and novelty of designs within the archive. The PDA will be a valuable resource for guiding development of protein design, helping the field reach its potential.

The PDA is available freely and without registration at https://pragmaticproteindesign.bio.ed.ac.uk/pda/.

sample_q_texts: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) function as regulators of protein-based activity by targeting cytoplasmic small RNAs. However, the mechanisms of miRNA action still remains undefined. Using adenine-depleted agarose scaffolds, we have recapitulated cellular functions that involve base pairing between the 5' and 3' halves of antisense strands and/or a 5' sequence element that performs binding and silencing of adjacent 3' oligomers. We are conducting both single nucleotide and multi-nucleotide binding protein cleavage assays to quantify the specificity and dynamics of miRNA action by mi-probes and paired 3'-cpi guides against a broad array of effector complexes. We demonstrate that complementation of bound complexes with dCas9 (1.5-pm ribonucleoprotein complexes) efficiently activates the whole complex, largely dependent on base pairing through 5' overhang binding and a presequence built in the second miRNA (or 3'-cpi guide) binding target. Also, we demonstrate that our system is significantly more sensitive, and more specific, than other approaches for capturing sequential human-like RNA binding. We conclude that dCas9 is an efficient tool for providing evidence in cellular mechanisms regulating both microRNA function and RNA guide specificities.

Characterizing the state of cellular gene expression is important for fundamental biological questions and drug discovery. Central to our understanding of cellular gene expression is the measurement of gene expression by a sensor such as a microRNA (miRNA) microarray (mcRNA) in situ. Unfortunately, the mapping of different microRNAs to experimentally observed cell types is not straightforward, especially for in-frame expression, and varying expression values for microRNAs at the genome scale. This, in turn, severely limits the use of all the microRNAs currently measured to model whole cell gene expression. Here, we introduce MetaboRNA to solve this problem by analyzing the functional relationships between miRNAs and the genomes of C. elegans and C. elegans brain cell types. We developed the MetaboRNA toolkit, a Python library for the robust construction and visualization of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) for microRNAs in C. elegans and can create networks that integrate information about the inter-microRNAs and genes, RNA families, and variants. Combining the network topology and expression data with RNA-seq and protein abundance measurements, we generate a MetaboRNA network that represents the knowledge of only miRNAs expressed from each source cell type. By addressing the two-sided missing-data problem of how to measure the expression level of microRNAs in diverse cell types, our approach generates network structures representing gene regulatory networks with consistent inter-cellular gene regulatory network topologies. We utilized our MetaboRNA toolkit in combination with microRNAs to infer the cellular network of miRNA from the MSK-1 genome, demonstrating the usefulness of the tools in tackling fundamental questions of cellular genomics. Our network designs were then validated using parallel data from HeLa cells, differentiating between small and larger miRNA lesions and validating the significance of residual miRNA variation between cells.

Strengths
• MetaboRNA network architectures in the MSK-1 cell type database with inter-microRNA and gene (RNA) coordinates.
• Unbiased estimation of microRNA expression across cell types with reliable genetic background information.
• Reliable modeling of miRNA expression in diverse cell types and cell types.
• MetaboRNA framework uses curated gene regulatory networks (GRNs) of cells and their inferred interactions.

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) recognize ~8% of all mRNA sequences. MiRNAs are essential regulators of gene expression by targeting mRNA sequences. Unlike most other miRNA targets, MicroRNAs require direct RNA interference to bind and be targeted. A gene-targeting pathway has been established in Drosophila melanogaster, which is called Lis1-ChIP. The Drosophila Lis1-ChIP pathway has been explored in numerous cases, including gene targeting, embryonic lethality, and female fertility. Despite its relevance to humans, the target locus of the Drosophila Lis1-ChIP pathway is not elucidated and no cellular target is clearly identified. We have applied tandem-sequencing to map the entire length of the Mis3L-Cus8 pathway, a small-RNA accessory that regulates the mis-processing of short RNA species to be processed by two microRNA types. Over 75% of the clones in the Mis3L-Cus8 overlap with the Lis1-ChIP locus, which is consistent with our being the Lis1-ChIP locus and both direct and indirect analogs of that homolog. Our findings establish the insect Mis3L-Cus8 homolog as a cis regulatory motif for the Drosophila Lis1-ChIP pathway. We propose a new model involving simultaneously hijacking both human and model insect Lis1-ChIP to complete a small-RNA cycle.

RNA editing in mammals is an essential process due to its essential function in maintaining protein stability, including maintaining protein expression. However, the relationship between RNA editing events, editing efficiencies, and RNA silencing pathways and regulatory networks in mammals is largely unresolved. We report in this review to report that RNA editing events, especially small single-nucleotide substitutions, are highly affected by RNA silencing pathways, including gene-silencing complexes. In addition, novel evidence has been highlighted in several key exons in exons 9 and 11 in the exons 16 and 19-exon and a few exons in the exons 3, 4, 10-14, and 19. That analysis reveals many of the novel small DNA-modification events in tandem DNA repeats (e.g., CG, TG, and GT), which are also called defined small editing sites (DSES). The findings may help to create a complete map of RNA editing in terms of coding and non-coding elements in human cells.

The translation of information from the genome into proteins, namely translation, is catalyzed by the ribosome. Translation is regulated by small RNAs: the small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). One such RNA, lncRNA c1b55i-derived nuclease (lincRNA), exhibits sequence complementarity with the translational start site of many genes. We hypothesized that lincRNAs could function as transcription factors that regulate translational competency of elongating ribosomes. To test our hypothesis, we characterized the proteome of C. elegans having the most conserved lincRNA binding sites. We characterized more than 74 3D structures of C. elegans lincRNAs and identified the use of as-yet-untranslated lincRNAs. I discovered a gene in vivo that is translated by uncapped ribosomal peptides and use as a template to generate c1b55i-derived nuclease. These results, in conjunction with previous observations that C. elegans truncates ribosomal protein synthesises in the absence of rRNA, and with biochemical data showing that ribosomal peptidase II is involved in ribosomal protein synthesis, provided definitive evidence that c1b55i-derived nuclease functions as a translational control factor.

HighlightsThe function of the Ribosomal Binding Site (RBS) is not well understood.
Newly discovered promoter and trans-activating potential of the RBS.
Short hairpin RNA-directed ribozyme inhibits translational initiation, but elongation is likely driven by spliceosomal activity.
Binding of stilt-mutant in vivo leaves open more potential positions for spliceosomal reactions.

Synaptins are highly conserved post-synaptic protein components in the central and nervous systems, and are primarily recruited as a fusion-partners of AMPARs and GABAA receptors in various synaptic processes. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) and non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) have been found to participate in numerous physiological processes, and gain and loss-of-function studies have demonstrated a role in various complex neurological disorders. In the CNS, microRNAs are shown to be involved in synapse-related gene expression and autism, as well as diseases characterized by neuronal development. Here, we exploited a microRNA cluster array and the electronic binding affinities of human microRNAs and investigated its expression in human neural progenitors and in mouse models of human neurodegeneration. Our results show a gene-gene interaction between a specific microRNA expression cluster (miR-120), whose antisense strand activated a gene known to be involved in the transcriptional and synaptic function of a coregulated gene with reduced activity (CCIMP), such as CCSC5 and GLIAS4. Expression of miR-120 was found in mouse ESCs that lacked miR-120, as well as mouse spinal cord interneurons that failed to transition to neurons and that were devoid of a synaptic function of a coregulated gene with reduced activity (CCIMP). In mouse hippocampal neurons, it was observed that miRNAs such as miR-120 activated a mRNA with high potential to function in the CNS. Higher concentrations of miR-120 compared to miR-9p, miR-30b, and miR-20a also activated the expression of key genes involved in neuronal differentiation and synaptic function. Taken together, our study suggests that an open miR-120-CCIMP circuit might have a role in the development of Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative diseases characterized by aberrant neuronal activity.

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs with major roles in post-transcriptional regulation and contribute to cell differentiation and tissue regeneration. While the miRNA-mRNA targets sequence is varied, it is conserved that host signaling plays a critical role in the regulation of miRNA-mRNA target pairing. To date, interactions between miRNA target sequences and different host proteins, pathways, and receptors have been identified for over 250 sites by the N400, a biophysics technique that studies neural activity in response to incoming information, in both mice and humans. While 200 of these targets are found in mRNA, 20% are present in miRNA and only 5% of them have a mRNA target when the mRNA is absent. However, since miRNAs and miRNAs are transcribed from the same transcriptome, they must simultaneously target the same protein. To account for this possibility, we examined whether RNAi-driven disruption of the 200 significant target sites would alter the expression of the up to 200 hosts that are target sites to different RNAi isoforms of each miRNA. Our findings indicate that the commonly used strategy of using miREx to target and knock down miRNA target sites can generate a wide range of protein functional effects due to the variability of miREx target sequences. In addition, we observed that RNase V enzymatic activity in terms of its ability to target a well-characterized mammalian target protein, SRS15, was also modulated by different miRNA target sites. Finally, RNase V still responded to miR4379-mediated miREx targeting; however, with only a minor percentage of targets affected. Taken together, these results are consistent with the hypothesis that diverse MiR4379-miR4379-mediated mimics are available in the human body, each with its target site-dependent effects and the ability to respond to a range of different targets based on the targets of their corresponding proteins.

Significance statementAlthough multiple mechanisms contribute to programmed cell death, the intrinsic significance of necrosis has recently been challenged by observations of microbial infection of mammalian cells. To characterize the underlying mechanisms, the context of necrosis has been reconsidered, and recent findings have challenged the dogma of necrosis as a self-sustaining state. We show that addition of a small number of nutrients, such as glucose, results in necrotic cell death. Thus, changes in nutrient-rich conditions, like those found in the lungs during the infection with the coronavirus, permit cells to proliferate and create a favorable environment for microbes. Our

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small noncoding RNA molecules that modulate many cellular functions, including gene expression. miRNAs primarily regulate gene expression at the post-transcriptional level, but the ability of miRNAs to control gene transcription is less well understood. In Drosophila, small regulatory RNA molecules (25-30 nt long with relatively simple structures) have been identified, but their effect on gene expression remains little understood. Here, we sequenced genes, identified the functional class of miRNAs expressed in neurons and identified target genes associated with 25 miRNA species that regulate six genes, one of which is proposed to form a crucial DNA-binding motif involved in miRNA control. We observed that small RNAs produced in the cytoplasm are translated from the RNA polymerase II regulatory domain to be incorporated into chromatin structures, thereby enhancing their potential for transcriptional regulation, allowing for a review of this phenotype across different species.

Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are small noncoding RNAs that are often proposed to regulate gene expression. The dynamics of circRNA levels is well-studied, but of the underlying mechanism, which links circRNA levels to changes in gene expression, we know very little. Here, we identify a functional connection between circRNA and protein translation, with investigators reporting that circ-5c isoforms correlate with translation of mRNAs in HEK293 cells. Using RNA-seq, we identified eight differentially abundant cDNAs with a circ-5c isoform that correlated with a previously studied long noncoding transcript. Analysis of the central pathway of translation - the c-Jun N-terminal kinase - highlights the importance of a functional link between circRNA and the signalling system of the CAP NAC transcription factor. Here, we report that circRNA levels are differentially regulated by different c-Jun isoforms, as well as the respective activator and inducers of the CAP NAC complex. We propose a non-redundant model for circRNA regulation of translation, which depends on c-Jun RNA binding. The identification of the functional link between circRNA and the protein translation system opens up a new target for genetic therapy by introducing therapeutic aptamers with modified circ-5c sequences to counteract the functional deficits in several diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease.

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are found in all known living cell types, from bacteria to human cells, and are key mediators of a vast array of biological processes including the RNA splicing of mRNAs, cell-to-cell cell identity, and much more. However, few studies have investigated the role of aberrant miRNA gene expression in neurodevelopment. Previously, we investigated the effect of posttranslational modification (PTM) of miR-206 in zebrafish neurodevelopment, leading to an understanding of how aberrant PTM of miR-206 generates non-autonomous mechanisms of neurodevelopment. We used epigenome-wide analysis to characterize the cumulative effects of miR-206 PTM and conclude that PTM represses miRNA-206 expression and promotes aberrant PTM, disrupting a number of neural pathways. These findings highlight the importance of PTM regulation in miRNA function and suggest that targeted therapeutic strategies involving miRNA-targeted therapeutics may be an effective tool for treating developmental dysregulation of the nervous system.
sample_p_texts: Post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression is essential for the correct development and functioning of an organism. This regulation is coordinated by a collection of proteins that work together to determine an RNAs post-transcriptional fate. Here, we provide a global overview of the RNA regulatory protein landscape in Caenorhabditis elegans, to provide insight into the coordination of post-transcriptional regulatory activities in the context of a multicellular organism. First, we have curated a comprehensive list of all known and putative RNA regulatory proteins encoded in the C. elegans genome, classified based on domain and functional annotations and published experimental data. Second, using protein-protein interaction data in the STRING database, we created a putative RNA regulatory protein interaction network that highlighted known RNA regulatory complexes, and leveraged this network to identify an additional 138 known and putative RNA regulators previously unannotated in C. elegans. Finally, we examined the tissue- and developmental-stage-specific expression of RNA regulators using published transcript expression data, which revealed strong expression in the gonad for a majority, as well as dozens expressed specifically in each of the major somatic C. elegans tissues. Taken together, this work will provide a valuable resource for future studies of RNA biology in C. elegans.

MicroRNAs (miRNA) are small non-coding RNAs that are key negative regulators of gene expression. Their roles include shaping the gene expression landscape during and after brain development by defining and maintaining levels of proteins that generate the distinct morphological and functional properties of neurons and other brain cell types. HT22, N2A, and SH-SY5Y are common immortalized neuronal cell lines that offer simple, less expensive, and time-saving options for in vitro modelling to evaluate miRNA functions. The extent to which these lines reflect primary neurons remains, however, unclear. Here, we benchmarked the miRNA profiles of cultured mouse hippocampal neurons against Argonaute-loaded miRNAs in the adult mouse hippocampus and miRNA data from the hippocampus of patients with drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy. We then compared the miRNA expression landscape in HT22, N2A and SH-SY5Y against mouse hippocampal primary cell cultures. We profiled over 700 miRNAs across the lines and detected 310 miRNAs in all four cell types. This included detection of neuron-enriched miRNAs such as miR-124 and miR-128, although the cell lines typically displayed lower levels of these than in primary neurons and reference adult hippocampal tissue. The miRNA profile in the HT22 cell line showed the highest correlation to the mouse primary neuronal cultures. Together, this study provides a dataset on basal miRNA expression across commonly used cell lines for neuroscience research and evidence for both conserved and distinct profiles that should be used to inform decisions on cell lines for modelling brain and miRNA research.

Argonaute proteins are essential players in RNA silencing pathways, and their N-terminal extensions, particularly in the PIWI clade, often harbor conserved sequences like RG motifs. Despite their prevalence in Argonaute proteins, the role of these motifs remains poorly understood. In this study, we focus on the RG motifs within the N-terminal region of Caenorhabditis elegans PRG-1, a PIWI clade Argonaute. Using sequence alignment across Caenorhabditis species, we identify three conserved RG motifs that are methylated, as confirmed by mass spectrometry. The region surrounding these motifs is intrinsically disordered, as predicted by disorder algorithms and structural modeling. While the RG motifs are critical for fertility, germline morphology, and piRNA silencing, they are not required for PRG-1 expression, localization, or piRNA loading. Notably, mutation of the RG motifs results in defects in downstream small RNA production, specifically the depletion of mutator class siRNAs, without affecting piRNA biogenesis. These findings suggest that the RG motifs of PRG-1 play a crucial role in linking piRNA-mediated silencing to siRNA production, and that their function is critical for fertility and germline maintenance in C. elegans. Despite these defects, the phenotypic severity in the RG mutant is milder than in a PRG-1 null mutant, highlighting the complexity of PRG-1 function and its post-translational modifications.

All eukaryotes possess the essential mRNA cap-binding protein eIF4E, which initiates translation. This protein is highly conserved, with versions from zebrafish and humans able to rescue yeast. All fish also have an additional eIF4E family, called eif4e1c, which is crucial for heart regeneration. Deletion of eif4e1c leads to growth defects and impaired heart regeneration, but its unclear if similar effects occur when canonical translation mechanisms are disrupted. In this study, we deleted the two zebrafish paralogs of eIF4E, eif4ea and eif4eb. While individual deletions of these genes do not show the same phenotypes as eif4e1c deletion, compound mutants enhanced eif4e1c phenotypes, suggesting partial compensation by canonical eIF4E proteins in eif4e1c mutants. Surprisingly, unlike other eukaryotes, deleting both canonical mRNA cap-binding proteins did not result in lethality, and eif4e1c could fully compensate for eIF4E function. Although we anticipated that double mutants would regenerate hearts better since they contain eif4e1c alone, no improvement was observed in the double mutant. Interestingly, single deletions of eif4ea or eif4eb did improve heart regeneration. This supports a model where the balance between the eif4e1c and canonical pathways is crucial for stimulating heart regeneration.

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small, non-coding RNA that play a critical role in regulating gene expressions that are important for a multitude of biological processes. In the preparation of miRNA sequencing libraries by using QIAseq miRNA library kit, adapter dimers might occur inadvertently and compromise the sequencing performance. In this technical note, we tested different adapter dilution strategies to minimise or diminish adapter dimers without compromising data quality. In our experiments, we found that RNA input amount plays a larger role in adapter dimer formation rather than the availability of the adapters itself. We suggest preparing the sequencing library with 10 times more RNA than the recommended input amount of the chosen protocol, e.g. following the adapter dilution and PCR cycle number of the standard 1 ng protocol with 10 ng RNA input. We also suggest analysing the data with deduplication by using unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) as it helps remove unusable reads.

A network analysis of canonical microRNA (miRNA) biogenesis identified DROSHA, Exportin-5, and DICER1 as essential proteins for both precursor and mature miRNA processing. The analysis revealed strong interactions between these proteins and others involved in miRNA biogenesis, suggesting a complex regulatory network. Ligand binding sites on these key proteins were identified, suggesting potential targets for therapeutic intervention. Our findings indicate that modulating miRNA biogenesis through these proteins could influence cellular protein production and function, providing a promising avenue for developing advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs) to impact protein expression in diseases such as cancer.

Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are a class of RNA with multiple functions, including the ability to be translated.

Several intrinsic features of circRNAs, such as high stability, confer them advantages over linear RNAs; therefore, circRNA-based drugs have recently received increasing attention.

However, the inefficiency of their cap-independent translation and the difficulties in the large-scale production of long circRNAs negatively impact on their use in therapy. Some efforts have been done to solve these issues related to circRNA adoption, but, to date, circRNA translation still relies on long IRESs (600-800) and chemical group addition. In this study, identified a 63-nt element able to drive circRNA translation comparably to the most commonly used IRESs. This element includes a a 13-nt sequence previously reported to enhance linear RNA translation and a segment of the UTR of the endogenously translated circRNA circZNF609. Notably, this element combines a comparable IRES-like efficiency to a considerably shorter length, expanding the landscape of ORFs potentially suitable for being translated from circRNAs and enhancing their potential as therapeutic agents in therapy.

In vitro transcribed messenger RNA (IVT mRNA) has emerged as a pivotal tool in mRNA-based therapies and has been extensively employed in gene function studies and genetic tool applications. However, the IVT process generates double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) by-products that are recognized by dsRNA sensors, triggering innate immune responses. In this study, we comprehensively analyzed the detrimental effects of dsRNA by-products on early zebrafish embryos, revealing that these by-products induce cell necrosis and delay maternal-zygotic transition by reducing global translation efficiency via Prkra, a recently identified dsRNA sensor in pluripotent cells. Importantly, we demonstrate that N1-methylpseudouridine (m1{varphi}) modification of IVT mRNAs effectively mitigates these adverse effects, as m1{varphi}-modified dsRNAs exhibit significantly lower binding affinity to the Prkra dimer. Our findings underscore a previously overlooked challenge in the use of IVT mRNA in early embryos and offer a robust solution to enhance the fidelity of mRNA applications. Furthermore, we elucidate that m1{varphi} modification minimizes the dsRNA-induced stress response in pluripotent cells through a distinct mechanism.

Toys are us (Trus) is the Drosophila melanogaster ortholog of mammalian Programmed Cell Death 2-Like (PDCD2L), a protein that has been implicated in ribosome biogenesis, cell cycle regulation, and oncogenesis. In this study, we examined the function of Trus during Drosophila development. CRISPR/Cas9 generated null mutations in trus lead to partial embryonic lethality, significant larval developmental delay, and complete pre-pupal lethality. In mutant larvae, we found decreased cell proliferation and growth defects in the brain and imaginal discs. Mapping relevant tissues for Trus function using trus RNAi and trus mutant rescue experiments revealed that imaginal disc defects are primarily responsible for the developmental delay, while the pre-pupal lethality is likely associated with faulty central nervous system (CNS) development. Examination of the molecular mechanism behind the developmental delay phenotype revealed that trus mutations induce the Xrp1-Dilp8 ribosomal stress-response in growth-impaired imaginal discs, and this signaling pathway attenuates production of the hormone ecdysone in the prothoracic gland. Additional Tap-tagging and mass spectrometry of components in Trus complexes isolated from Drosophila Kc cells identified Ribosomal protein subunit 2 (RpS2), which is coded by string of pearls (sop) in Drosophila, and Eukaryotic translation elongation factor 1 alpha 1 (eEF11) as interacting factors. We discuss the implication of these findings with respect to the similarity and differences in trus genetic null mutant phenotypes compared to the haplo-insufficiency phenotypes produced by heterozygosity for mutants in Minute genes and other genes involved in ribosome biogenesis.

Authors SummaryRibosomes are essential macromolecular machines required for decoding mRNA to make proteins, the major biomolecules that carry out all central cellular functions. As such, their structural and operational integrity is critical to organismal survival, and mutations that disrupt proper stoichiometry or assembly of ribosomes produce serious pathological consequences during an organisms development and/or adult life. The ribosome assembly factor PDCD2L is highly conserved from yeast to man, yet its overall function and requirement during development is poorly understood. By examining the developmental consequences of null mutations in trus, which encodes the Drosophila PDCD2L homolog, we demonstrate an essential role for this factor in cell-cycle regulation. Furthermore, disruption of Trus function in mitotically dividing imaginal tissue activates the Xrp1-dilp8 stress response pathway which limits production of ecdysone, the major arthropod molting hormone, leading to severe developmental delay during larval stages. These studies provide new insights on the requirements of this highly conserved ribosome assemble factor during development.
